sentences.text: "There are two kinds of customers," Uncle Tomáš said, later that afternoon.
"Normal customers.
Their clock is broken.
They want it fixed.
Simple work.
I do it, they pay, they go." He paused.
"And there are the other customers." "What are they," said Klara.
"They are people," said Uncle Tomáš, "who have a stopped clock.
But their clock is not really the problem.
Their clock stopped because something else stopped.
Something in their life.
And they think, if they can just fix the clock, maybe the other thing will fix too."
"Does that work," Klara asked.
Uncle Tomáš thought about it.
He said, "Sometimes.
Not exactly the way they hope.
But sometimes." He was quiet for a moment.
Then he said, "That is the harder work.
I have to do the clock.
But I also have to talk to the customer.

Because if I only fix the clock and I do not talk to the customer, then the clock is fixed and the customer is not, and the customer will bring the clock back in three months saying it has stopped again.
And it will not really have stopped.
They will only think it has."
"How do you know which one is which," Klara asked.
"How they walk in," said Uncle Tomáš.
"How they hold the clock.
How they set it down.
Whether they look at it or at me.
It is not hard to tell.
You will see.
If someone like that comes in this week, you can watch.
But you have to be quiet.
Do not ask questions during the visit.
After they go, we can talk about it.
Yes?" Klara nodded.
She thought she understood.
For two days after that, nobody came in who was a special customer.
There were a few normal ones — a woman who dropped off a wall clock that had stopped chiming, a young man who wanted a battery for his cheap watch.
Klara helped a little.
Uncle Tomáš taught her how to open the back of a pocket watch with the small brass tool, and how to name some of the parts — the mainspring, the balance wheel, the escapement.
It was slow careful work, and Klara was surprised to find that she liked it.
The woman came on Wednesday afternoon.
Klara noticed her right away.
She was maybe fifty years old and she wore a grey coat and a red scarf and she was holding something against her chest with both hands.
She came in and stopped at the door and did not walk any further.
She looked at Uncle Tomáš.
She did not say anything.
Uncle Tomáš rose slowly from the bench.
He did not say anything either.
He walked over to her.
He did not reach for what she was holding.
He said, in a very gentle voice, "Come and sit down." He led her to a small chair beside the workbench.
He looked at Klara.
He said, softly, in Czech-accented English so the woman would not understand, "Watch.
Quiet." And Klara nodded.
She had understood already.
This was one of the other customers.
The woman opened the small wooden box she had been carrying.
Inside was a silver pocket watch.
She took it out.
She held it in the palms of both her hands.
She held it out to Uncle Tomáš, but he did not take it right away.
He said, "When did it stop?" The woman said, in Czech, "Three years and four months ago.
On the ninth of July.
At 3:47 in the morning." She looked down at the watch.
"That is when my husband died.
He was wearing it that night.
It stopped at that moment.
It has not run since."
Uncle Tomáš nodded.
He did not say anything.
He waited.
The woman held the watch out for another moment.
Then she said, "My daughter is getting married next month.
She asked if she could carry it.
In her flowers.
Something of her father with her.
I said yes.
But it has to be running.
It has to be a watch again.
Not a — not a stopped thing." She stopped.
She was trying not to cry.
Uncle Tomáš finally reached forward and took the watch, very carefully.
He held it in his palm.
He did not open it yet.
He looked at her.
He said, "May I ask you something.
Are you sure you want it running." The woman looked up.
"I am not sure," she said.
"That is what I have been thinking about for three years.
That is why I did not bring it before." Uncle Tomáš nodded slowly.
"That is the right thing to think about," he said.
"When it starts running, you do not get this exact watch back.
You get a similar one.
It is a watch that runs.
That is a different thing than a watch that stopped at 3:47 on the ninth of July."
The woman was crying now, quietly, without wiping her eyes.
She said, "I know.
I have thought about that.
I want to have both.
Somehow.
But I know I cannot." Uncle Tomáš said, "You can have both.
In a way.
Come back on Saturday morning.
I will show you what I mean." The woman nodded.
She stood up.
She thanked him.
She left.
Klara did not move from her stool until the door closed and the little bell stopped ringing.
